hints.quote: If you need to know anything at all in endocrinology, diabetes is the one that you want to know. In the exams, diabetes takes a very big chunk of assessment.
hints.take: Expect this lecture to carry many of the 45 new-material questions: know every class's mechanism and main side effects, and insulin, metformin, the GLP-1 agonists and the SGLT2 inhibitors in depth.

hints.quote: It's common to have questions that ask you, someone is planning to eat something, and what type of insulin they need.
hints.take: Mealtime coverage needs a fast insulin (rapid analogs or regular); NPH starts in 2 to 4 hours and glargine is basal.

hints.quote: The other part would be maybe some calculations about units and how they are given. I don't think you would need that.
hints.take: Skip insulin dose arithmetic; know the preparations, their timing and basal versus bolus use.

hints.quote: Any drug that works by stimulating insulin release will have this same side effect of hypoglycemia.
hints.take: Insulin, sulfonylureas and meglitinides cause hypoglycemia; the rest rarely do on their own.

hints.quote: When you are comparing different drugs for diabetes, those are the things we're always looking at. Which one will not cause hypoglycemia? Which one will not cause weight gain? I've said it, like, a thousand times now.
hints.take: For every class, know its hypoglycemia risk and its weight effect.

hints.quote: Metformin is very important, because so far it is still the first-line drug for anyone who is newly diagnosed with diabetes.
hints.take: Metformin is first-line unless a comorbidity (weight, heart failure, cardiovascular disease) points to a GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor.

hints.quote: If it's normal, metformin will not bring it lower.
hints.take: Metformin has no effect at normal glucose, so its hypoglycemia risk is very low.

hints.quote: In fact, that's an absolute contraindication. When the GFR is less than 30, we do not give them metformin.
hints.take: eGFR below 30 means stop metformin.

hints.quote: This drug will only work in people who have a functional pancreas, who are still able to make insulin.
hints.take: Secretagogues fail when beta cells are gone (for example when C-peptide is absent).

hints.quote: C-peptide level will always tell you if they are making insulin at all, or if they are not making.
hints.take: Absent C-peptide in a patient on insulin means no insulin of their own.

hints.quote: If you're going to be expecting questions, especially in your board exam, watch out for insulin, watch out for GLPs, watch out for the sodium glucose transport inhibitors. Metformin being the first-line drug.
hints.take: Prioritize insulin, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors and metformin, and situational choices among them.

hints.quote: If somebody has a weight problem, obviously everybody here should know that GLP will be the first-line drug.
hints.take: Obesity plus new type 2 diabetes points to a GLP-1 agonist such as semaglutide.

hints.quote: Somebody has a cardiovascular problem and you give them diuretics to help them pee, and now they have newly diagnosed diabetes. Why won't you consider something like Farxiga?
hints.take: Heart failure plus diabetes points to an SGLT2 inhibitor; dapagliflozin is FDA approved to treat heart failure.

hints.quote: This drug is only recommended now for people who don't have any cardiovascular issues, because of the tendency to cause edema.
hints.take: TZDs cause edema and heart failure; contraindicated in NYHA class III or IV.

hints.quote: Which class may increase the risk of macular edema? I'm sure I skipped it, so I didn't mention it, but it's right there in the slide.
hints.take: Thiazolidinediones are the class linked to macular edema.

hints.quote: People who have a history of thyroid cancer have been advised not to try the drug.
hints.take: All GLP-1 agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors.

hints.quote: Micro is the one that involves neuropathy, nephropathy, and retinopathy. Those three are very important to know.
hints.take: Microvascular: neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy. Macrovascular: coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, stroke.

hints.quote: Regular and intermediate have been around for a long time, so they are available over the counter, so you should know that.
hints.take: Regular insulin and NPH can be bought without a prescription.

hints.quote: In emergency, the drug of choice is glucagon.
hints.take: Conscious patient: fast sugar by mouth. Emergency: glucagon by injection or nasal spray.

hints.quote: We have four parameters here, and you need two.
hints.take: Diagnosis needs two agreeing results: A1C 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 or more, OGTT 200 or more, random above 200.

hints.quote: Do I want to bother you with all of this? Maybe not.
hints.take: For the TZDs, know PPAR-gamma (a nuclear receptor) and the effects, not the gene details.

hints.quote: The alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: not very widely used anymore... I don't know many people who still use Symlin.
hints.take: Know acarbose and pramlintide in outline: mechanism, the main adverse effect, and when they cause hypoglycemia.

hints.quote: Bile acid sequestrants are not very popular drugs for diabetes. We have gone past the use of some of these classes.
hints.take: Colesevelam: barely absorbed, binds other drugs, can raise triglycerides; bromocriptine is only listed.

hints.quote: In the clinical trial, several other things were reported, like fracture risk... Those are kind of some rare things that were reported during the clinical trial. But okay, yeah, it's here. It's actually a black box warning. Risk of amputation.
hints.take: Don't memorize the SGLT2 warnings drug by drug; know the class's infections, polyuria and hypotension, and the boxed warning for amputation.

hints.quote: If it's secondary, the pituitary is overproducing the TSH, causing a secondary increase in the T3 and T4, so both of them will be elevated. That's like a typical question in anything. T3, T4 high, TSH low, that's primary; both high, that's secondary. And this applies to any other organ where there's communication with the pituitary gland.
hints.take: Expect a lab-pattern question. Opposite directions (hormone vs TSH) = primary, the gland itself; same direction = secondary, the pituitary. Practice all four thyroid patterns and the same rule for ACTH and cortisol.

hints.quote: Whenever we use the word primary, it means it's coming from the organ that produces this specific hormone. Secondary means it responds to a stimulus from elsewhere.
hints.take: Know the definitions, not just the patterns: secondary hyperthyroidism is a pituitary overproducing TSH.

hints.quote: Very similar to thyroid. Primary hyperthyroidism, T3, T4 high, TSH low. Primary Cushing, cortisol high, and the ACTH low. Secondary, both will be high. (Part 2, about 20 minutes into the 2 pm hour)
hints.take: He repeated the rule the next hour, so a corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease) should read as ACTH high and cortisol high.

hints.quote: It's important to know that they can be multifocal, because the treatment for PTC is different than the treatment of FTC. If we diagnose FTC, a hemithyroidectomy is enough. If you have PTC, you have to take the entire thyroid gland, because the other lobe might have another focus.
hints.take: Papillary = multifocal = total thyroidectomy; follicular = hemithyroidectomy is enough.

hints.quote: In our world, when we see a neoplasm in the thyroid, it's very important to know: is it due to a RAS mutation, or is it due to a BRAF mutation? It's not on the slides, but that's the real-life practice.
hints.take: BRAF = papillary, spreads by lymphatics to nodes; RAS = follicular, spreads by blood vessels to distant organs; RET = medullary. This is from the recording only.

hints.quote: Most importantly, they have hypochromasia. Not hyper, hypo. They're a bit more whitish. They called them Orphan Annie eye nuclei.
hints.take: Papillary carcinoma nuclei are PALE, enlarged and overcrowded, with grooves and pseudoinclusions. A stem saying "hyperchromatic" is the trap.

hints.quote: Whenever we see a true psammoma body in the thyroid, the presumption, of course, is that this is a PTC.
hints.take: Psammoma bodies = laminated calcifications of dead papillae = papillary carcinoma (present in about half of cases).

hints.quote: The most common cause of an ectopic production of ADH is small cell carcinoma of the lung. These patients will come with hyponatremia.
hints.take: SIADH: low sodium, small cell lung cancer. DI is the opposite: high sodium, dilute urine.

hints.quote: Just remembering its name kind of helps you out with the symptoms. If it's an antidiuretic thing and you have a deficiency of it, you'll have a lot of diuresis.
hints.take: No ADH = polyuria (diabetes insipidus); too much ADH = water retention and hyponatremia (SIADH). The same trick works for the pituitary cells: the name says the hormone.

hints.quote: Unlike the autoantibodies in Graves that stimulate TSH, these ones block TSH.
hints.take: As taught, Graves and Hashimoto both target the TSH receptor: Graves stimulates it, Hashimoto blocks it.

hints.quote: This is one of the emergencies we have. If they took a biopsy for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, you want to tell them immediately and send it for molecular testing, to hopefully get something they can target.
hints.take: Anaplastic carcinoma: rapidly fatal unless a targetable mutation (such as BRAF) is found.

hints.quote: Any tumor that goes the angioinvasion route, the main four organs they metastasize to are liver, lung, bone and brain.
hints.take: Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood; the slide names lung and bones (shoulder girdle, sternum, skull, iliac bones).

hints.quote: Empty sella syndrome... you don't need to know all of the details, but occasionally the sella turcica just doesn't have the pituitary gland.
hints.take: Know empty sella as a cause of hypopituitarism (classically obese multiparous women); skip the anatomy of the diaphragma sellae.

hints.quote: I'm not specifically sure why they would have a large tongue in response to hypothyroidism, but that's what happens.
hints.take: Know the enlarged tongue in myxedema and cretinism (an oral finding) without a mechanism.

hints.quote: They sit behind the thyroid gland, not anterior to it. Behind.
hints.take: The parathyroids are posterior to the thyroid, which is why a thyroidectomy can take them out.

hints.quote: A way to remember how much fat versus how much cells is by age. If you are in your 70s, 70 percent of the parathyroid should be fat, and 30 percent should be your neuroendocrine cells.
hints.take: Expected percent of cells is about 100 minus the age. A gland at 70 to 80 percent cells in a middle-aged or older person is hypercellular and may be hyperfunctioning.

hints.quote: The way to remember the classic triad is stones, bones and groans.
hints.take: Kidney stones, bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica) and neuromuscular complaints, though most patients now are found on routine labs with no symptoms.

hints.quote: Adenomas and hyperplasias cannot be distinguished only on lab testing. It's purely based on whether it's a single nodule or multiple.
hints.take: Both raise PTH and calcium. One enlarged gland means adenoma; several mean hyperplasia.

hints.quote: The amount of hypercalcemia would be so much that the calcium levels tend to be over 13.
hints.take: Parathyroid carcinoma: very high, symptomatic calcium, an ill-defined invasive mass, pleomorphic nuclei and necrosis. Very rare: he has probably seen one.

hints.quote: If the surgery is effective, the amount of parathyroid hormone will drop more than 50 percent.
hints.take: Intraoperative PTH: a fall of more than 50 percent, not a normal value, means the gland is out. It works because PTH lasts minutes.

hints.quote: Before that testing used to be done, they used to send it to us. Now everything is easier.
hints.take: Frozen section was the old way to confirm parathyroid tissue during surgery; intraoperative PTH has largely replaced it.

hints.quote: The most important is to solve the primary issue. Once you fix the vitamin D deficiency, calcium goes to normal, parathyroid goes to normal.
hints.take: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is treated at its cause (renal failure, calcium or vitamin D deficiency); surgery, if needed, is three and a half glands.

hints.quote: Dental root hypoplasia, important, no calcium.
hints.take: A dental finding of hypoparathyroidism, alongside cataracts, spotty alopecia, nail fragility and basal ganglia calcification.

hints.quote: There are two physical exam tests: Chvostek and Trousseau sign.
hints.take: Chvostek: tap the cheek, the face twitches. Trousseau: compress the arm, the hand spasms. Both mean low calcium.

hints.quote: Pseudo means false. The parathyroid hormones are produced just fine, but the organ is not responding.
hints.take: Pseudohypoparathyroidism: PTH high, calcium low, phosphate high. (He said "kidney failure" while explaining it; true renal failure is a look-alike to rule out.)

hints.quote: It gets sweeter as you go from outside to inside. Salt, sugar, sex.
hints.take: Glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens), from the outside in.

hints.quote: Very similar to thyroid. Primary hyperthyroidism, T3, T4 high, TSH low. Primary Cushing, cortisol high and the ACTH low. Secondary, both will be high.
hints.take: Read cortisol with ACTH. He said "cortisone" in places; the hormone is cortisol.

hints.quote: The renin would be low, aldosterone would be high. The same concept repeats itself, primary versus secondary.
hints.take: Conn syndrome: renin low. Renal artery stenosis, CHF or a renin-secreting tumor: renin high. Aldosterone is high in both.

hints.quote: The treatment for all congenital adrenal hyperplasia is glucocorticoids, because they utilize the same concept of negative feedback.
hints.take: Glucocorticoid lowers ACTH, which quiets the whole pathway and the androgen excess.

hints.quote: There is this diagram that I had to memorize when I did my exams.
hints.take: He showed the whole steroid pathway but taught only what the 21- and 17-hydroxylase blocks do. Know those two.

hints.quote: Most adenomas are non-secreting, but the secreting ones are usually aldosterone.
hints.take: Functional adrenal cortical adenoma = aldosterone (high sodium, low potassium, hypertension). Virilizing adrenal tumor = usually carcinoma.

hints.quote: The numbers have stayed for over the last 20 years, so that might be a bit not accurate. Could be true, could be not.
hints.take: The rule of 10s is approximate, but it is what the slide teaches: 10 percent familial, extra-adrenal, bilateral and malignant.

hints.quote: The first person who described it was German, so he described the pattern as Zellballen, which means the balls.
hints.take: Pheochromocytoma (and paraganglioma) cells grow in nests or balls: Zellballen.

hints.quote: Whenever you hear the word blast, it means it's the precursor, or the immature form of the cells.
hints.take: Neuroblastoma is a primitive, very aggressive childhood tumor (80 percent under 5); adults get olfactory neuroblastoma in the roof of the nose.

hints.quote: In class, Dr. Herr told the class to focus on slides 8-10, 12 and 19-21 of this lecture.
hints.take: Not on the posted recording; from the class. Slides 8-10: the Sertoli cell (its shape, the occluding junctions and the blood-testis barrier, FSH, its jobs); 12: the Leydig cells, outside the tubules; 19-21: the three spermatogonia and the clonal path from spermatogonium to sperm, and the labeled tubule. The hub's High Likelihood questions for this lecture start with them.

hints.quote: This image is actually on your exam, so I do want you to know the labels on this image, so make sure you pay attention to it, and you'll be able to answer at least one question, if not a few questions.
hints.take: Learn the labeled Sertoli cell drawing from the basal lamina to the lumen: type A and type B spermatogonia, the junctional complex, primary spermatocyte, early and late spermatids, and the two compartments.

hints.quote: So you need to know the difference between those two, right? This basal compartment here from the adluminal compartment here. Adluminal meaning near the lumen.
hints.take: Spermatogonia sit in the basal compartment, below the Sertoli cells' tight junctions; primary spermatocytes and spermatids develop in the adluminal compartment, behind the blood-testis barrier.

hints.quote: I'm not going to test you on any specific images that are stained images, but you will see cartoon images.
hints.take: Don't memorize how micrographs look; know the drawings and what each structure is, where it sits and what it does.

hints.quote: The only two components that I really think you should know about in terms of the spermatic cord is this testicular artery, which is supplying the testes with blood, and there's this thing called a pampiniform plexus of veins.
hints.take: Spermatic cord: the ductus deferens plus the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus of veins.

hints.quote: Sertoli cells are going to produce the secretions that aid in sperm nourishment and transport ... just know that they are the refrigerator, right? They're nourishment and transport.
hints.take: Sertoli cells support and feed the germ cells, phagocytose shed cytoplasm, make ABP, inhibin and anti-Müllerian hormone, and form the blood-testis barrier.

hints.quote: The luteinizing hormone is going to bind to receptors on the Leydig cells ... and that will initiate the production of testosterone, which stimulates sperm development. Follicle-stimulating hormone will stimulate the production of androgen-binding protein from Sertoli cells.
hints.take: Keep the two chains apart: LH, Leydig, testosterone; FSH, Sertoli, androgen-binding protein.

hints.quote: You've heard it a lot, but here it is again. Release of luteinizing hormone is inhibited by a feedback loop in which testosterone lowers luteinizing hormone secretion.
hints.take: Testosterone is the brake on LH; inhibin from the Sertoli cells is the brake on FSH.

hints.quote: It's estimated to take 74 days for spermatogenesis to be completed, so it's not an immediate thing.
hints.take: About 74 days in the tubules, then 2 to 12 days of maturation in the epididymis (Dr. Madison's physiology lecture says about two months).

hints.quote: Seminal vesicles make up the majority of the semen, of the semen volume, 70%. They're rich in fructose, energy, prostaglandins, and proteins.
hints.take: Seminal vesicles: about 70 percent of the volume, fructose for energy, and the lipochrome pigment that fluoresces under UV light.

hints.quote: It's wrapped around the urethra. I think that's something to consider. So, if a patient comes in and says they're having issues urinating, or it takes them a really long time to urinate, it could be compression of the prostate gland around that urethra.
hints.take: An enlarged prostate compresses the urethra it wraps around; expect a patient who has trouble urinating.

hints.quote: Bulbourethral glands, the only thing that you can take away, really, from this image is that it has this skeletal muscle. So skeletal muscle is under autonomic control or somatic control? ... Yeah, somatic.
hints.take: Bulbourethral glands: skeletal muscle between the units, so somatic (voluntary) control; their galactose and sialic acid mucus lubricates before the emission of semen.

hints.quote: If we had a corpus cavernosum around the urethra, there wouldn't be many human beings.
hints.take: The two corpora cavernosa fill with blood; the corpus spongiosum around the urethra fills much less, so the urethra stays open.

hints.quote: It's always point and shoot. So it's parasympathetic for pointing and sympathetic for shooting.
hints.take: Erection is parasympathetic; ejaculation is sympathetic.

hints.quote: You don't need to know this image necessarily.
hints.take: For the erectile tissue's blood supply figure, know the mechanism (smooth muscle relaxes, the corpora cavernosa fill, the veins are compressed), not the labels of every vessel.

hints.quote: This image has no relevance to you because you need to see another image to understand it.
hints.take: Skip the prostatic utricle figure; know that the ejaculatory ducts pass through the prostate to the urethra.

hints.quote: In class, Dr. Herr told the class to focus on slides 18-21, 30-31, 33-34 and 38-39 of this lecture.
hints.take: Not on the posted recording; from the class. Slides 18-21: the secondary (antral) and Graafian follicles; 30-31: the uterine tube's cells; 33-34: the uterine wall's layers and the endometrium; 38-39: the endometrium's layers during menstruation. The hub's High Likelihood questions for this lecture start with them.

hints.quote: All follicles within the ovary contain a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I. The LH surge drives this process. The secondary oocyte enters meiosis II and arrests at metaphase II until fertilization.
hints.take: Two arrests, two releases: prophase I until the LH surge, metaphase II until fertilization (his three-asterisk slide).

hints.quote: I just want to show you this one more time. So FSH surge induces growth, but we need LH to kind of trigger maturation and ovulation of the dominant oocyte.
hints.take: FSH grows the 10 to 12 antral follicles; LH, in the FSH plus LH surge, matures and ovulates the dominant one.

hints.quote: The process of going from this primordial follicle to a mature follicle takes many months. This is not the same as the 28 to 33 day cycle. This takes many, many months to occur.
hints.take: Primordial to Graafian takes many months, far longer than one cycle.

hints.quote: The female will contain 5 to 7 million primary oocytes. That's pretty wild. 5 to 7 million of these primary oocytes.
hints.take: Know the falling numbers: 5 to 7 million by the 5th fetal month, 1 to 2 million at birth, about 400,000 at menarche, about 450 ovulated.

hints.quote: There's a granulosa layer, a very small basement membrane, a theca interna, and a theca externa, so you can demarcate those on a histological slide.
hints.take: Be ready to name the Graafian follicle's wall from the antrum out: granulosa, basement membrane, theca interna, theca externa.

hints.quote: The major components of ZP are glycoproteins, ZP1, 2, and 3. You don't need to know those, that's fine.
hints.take: Know that the zona pellucida is glycoprotein made by the follicular cells, and that oocyte microvilli and granulosa filopodia meet through it; skip the ZP names.

hints.quote: There are external genitalia, for example, the labial folds, the clitoris, and the vestibule, which we will not discuss.
hints.take: Skip the external genitalia (and the broad ligament's 3D anatomy, which he also passes over).

hints.quote: Estrogen kind of stays low, and then around day 7 it's going to start to rise. It'll peak around day 12 or 13. Progesterone stays pretty low, and then kind of gradually at day 14 increases to about a peak at day 22.
hints.take: Read the graph by day: estrogen peaks about day 12 or 13, just before the LH surge; progesterone peaks about day 22, from the corpus luteum.

hints.quote: FSH levels are kind of baseline, and then they're gonna dip just a little bit, and then they're gonna peak right here, right before ovulation. Luteinizing hormone: baseline, big peak with FSH.
hints.take: On his graph FSH peaks with LH just before ovulation (days 13 to 15). The hub follows his graph in every lecture; L16's slide says inhibin holds FSH down then.

hints.quote: The wave of cilia is directed towards the uterus. These non-ciliated peg cells will secrete fluid that provides nutrient to the ovum. So I do want you to know some components of this.
hints.take: Know the tube's two cell types (ciliated cells beating toward the uterus, peg cells feeding the ovum), its folds in every region and its poorly defined muscularis.

hints.quote: There's periodic contractions of the spiral artery that are triggered by a reduction in progesterone. They deprive the supply of oxygen, so they create hypoxia in the functional layer.
hints.take: Menstruation: progesterone falls, the spiral arteries constrict, the functionalis goes hypoxic and sheds.

hints.quote: The basal layer, again, is not really affected, because these basal straight arteries provide independent blood supply to the basal layer.
hints.take: Spiral arteries feed the functionalis; straight arteries feed the basalis, which is why it survives and regrows the lining.

hints.quote: During pregnancy, the cervical secretions are more viscous, and they form a plug to prevent entry of microorganisms and sperm into the uterus, so that's really fascinating.
hints.take: Cervix in pregnancy: a viscous mucus plug; and its abrupt switch to stratified squamous where it meets the vagina is the transformation zone.

hints.quote: Colostrum is produced for 3 to 4 days after birth. Colostrum has increased concentration of proteins and immunoglobulin A, so IgA.
hints.take: Colostrum: the first 3 to 4 days, more protein and IgA; prolactin makes milk, oxytocin ejects it.

hints.quote: This is where I would study. Being able to compare and contrast Sertoli cells and Leydig cells is really important for this lecture.
hints.take: Make a two-column list and know it cold: Sertoli (tubule wall, FSH, nourishment, blood-testis barrier, ABP, inhibin, aromatase, spermiation, AMH in the fetus) against Leydig (interstitium, LH, testosterone).

hints.quote: What you need to know is that in development, when AMH is not around, you're going to develop these Müllerian ducts. ... That's an important piece to remember.
hints.take: AMH from the Sertoli cells makes the Müllerian ducts regress; without it, a uterus forms. It works even in androgen insensitivity, which is why neither disorder has a uterus.

hints.quote: They are responsible for synthesizing testosterone. That's their major contribution. Worth remembering.
hints.take: Leydig cells, in the interstitium, make testosterone from cholesterol under LH.

hints.quote: That's an old way of thinking. ... You can cross this out and put it in red. ... Leydig cells have some, but Sertoli cells from fetal development onward are really going to produce most of that aromatase activity.
hints.take: If a question asks where aromatase is, answer the Sertoli cells (turned up by FSH) at every age, not the Leydig cells his slide names for adults.

hints.quote: FSH is preferentially going to bind to Sertoli cells. It's not to say that the Leydig cells don't have FSH receptors, but the Sertoli cells have a high expression of FSH receptors. And then LH is going to preferentially bind to the Leydig cells.
hints.take: FSH goes with Sertoli and LH with Leydig; both receptors are Gs-coupled and work through PKA.

hints.quote: So testosterone turns off luteinizing hormone at the anterior pituitary, inhibin turns off FSH.
hints.take: Each testis cell brakes its own gonadotropin: Leydig testosterone on GnRH and LH, Sertoli inhibin on FSH.

hints.quote: Inhibin specifically doesn't feed back to the hypothalamus. It's only going to feed back to the gonadotropes and turn off FSH.
hints.take: Inhibin acts at the pituitary only; testosterone acts at both the hypothalamus (GnRH) and the pituitary (mainly LH).

hints.quote: We're gonna spend most of our time here today talking about spermatogenesis, how we form sperm.
hints.take: Know the cell order (spermatogonia, primary and secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), four haploid spermatids with 23 chromosomes each, and that maturation finishes in the epididymis.

hints.quote: Really optimal spermatogenesis is happening at about 34 degrees Celsius.
hints.take: Use 34 degrees Celsius for this lecture (Dr. Herr's L13 says about 35); warm, the testes hang lower, cold, the scrotum tightens and pulls them up.

hints.quote: One thing I want to point out is this acrosome region here. ... A lot of proteolytic enzymes and a lot of hyaluronidases that are going to allow for the penetration of the sperm into the egg.
hints.take: The acrosome comes from the Golgi and carries the enzymes that get the sperm through the egg's layers; the midpiece's mitochondria power the tail.

hints.quote: There's a kind of a crude mnemonic, but it works. ... It's called point and shoot. ... Point, parasympathetic; shoot, sympathetic. It's crude, but you'll remember it. That's one thing you don't forget.
hints.take: Erection and lubrication are parasympathetic; emission and ejaculation are sympathetic.

hints.quote: An important vessel to remember are these cavernosal arteries, because these are what's going to drive erection, essentially.
hints.take: Nitric oxide from parasympathetic nerves dilates the cavernosal arteries; the engorged tissue then compresses the veins.

hints.quote: There are drugs that target the enzymes that break down cyclic GMP. ... That's done by phosphodiesterase 5. And in the case of sildenafil, Viagra, those drugs target that phosphodiesterase.
hints.take: NO activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP; sildenafil blocks PDE5 so cGMP stays high.

hints.quote: Not a lot of information here. I was just trying to show you the interaction between the Sertoli cells and the sperm.
hints.take: Nothing extra to learn from the picture slide of Sertoli cells wrapped around sperm; know what Sertoli cells do.

hints.quote: High yield for exam, right? Compare and contrast luteal versus follicular.
hints.take: Make the two-column table: follicular (days 0 to 14, proliferative, the growing follicle, estrogen, the lining grows, watery stretchy mucus that helps sperm, estradiol's negative feedback, working toward fertilization) against luteal (days 14 to 28, secretory, the corpus luteum, progesterone, proliferation slows, more vessels and glycogen, thick mucus, a slight rise in temperature, working toward implantation).

hints.quote: Very important slide. I'd know this slide pretty well, because this is showing you who's responding to what, kind of like we have with our Sertoli and Leydig cells.
hints.take: FSH binds the granulosa cells (they carry the FSH receptors) and turns up aromatase, so testosterone becomes 17-beta estradiol. LH binds the theca cells, which make some progesterone and a lot of testosterone and have no aromatase; that testosterone moves to the granulosa cells. Theca is like Leydig, granulosa like Sertoli.

hints.quote: I don't care that you know, again, all the enzymes involved, just know the regulatory points. ... But remember these two steps.
hints.take: LH turns up cholesterol desmolase (P450scc), the rate-limiting step, cholesterol to pregnenolone, in the theca cells; FSH turns up aromatase, testosterone to 17-beta estradiol, in the granulosa cells. Aromatase is in males too, but far more active in females.

hints.quote: I don't care that you know most of those enzymes unless we're talking about aromatase or cholesterol desmolase.
hints.take: Skip the rest of the steroid pathway's enzymes; know the two he named and which hormone and cell each belongs to.

hints.quote: By and large, progesterone is going to be a negative feedback regulator. ... Estrogens is unique. The majority of the time, it is a negative feedback regulator. There's one point in the menstrual cycle where it becomes a positive feedback regulator.
hints.take: Progesterone: negative only. Estradiol: negative through the follicular phase, positive at midcycle once it passes about 200 pg/mL.

hints.quote: In females of reproductive years, the predominant estrogen is going to be estradiol, 17-beta estradiol. During pregnancy, the predominant estrogen is going to be estriol. And then during menopause, the predominant estrogen is estrone.
hints.take: Three estrogens, three stages of life: estradiol (reproductive years, the ovary), estriol (pregnancy), estrone (menopause).

hints.quote: Remember this, though, because this is during menopause. ... That DHEA, remember, is coming from that adrenal cortex. ... That's where we're getting a lot of our postmenopausal estrogens from.
hints.take: After menopause the estrogen is estrone, made from adrenal DHEA, and it is not nearly as potent as estradiol.

hints.quote: Those follicular cells will differentiate into a cell population called the granulosa cells, okay? Remember those cells, because those are going to be important. ... They're called the theca cells. Okay, another, the second important cell to remember.
hints.take: Primary follicle: the follicular cells around the oocyte become cuboidal granulosa cells. Secondary follicle: the granulosa cells proliferate into many layers and theca cells appear on the outside.

hints.quote: There's some intermediate phases in there as well. I don't care as much about that. ... Just know that one of them is going to become the dominant follicle.
hints.take: Don't memorize the names of the in-between follicles (tertiary or antral); know the order, that several grow each cycle, that one Graafian follicle becomes dominant and releases the egg, and that the rest regress.

hints.quote: What happens is estrogen levels get so high that there's a switch that happens. ... It switches from a negative feedback regulator to a positive feedback regulator. So it kind of reaches this critical level, give or take 200 picograms per mil, and that actually stimulates ... a surge of LH.
hints.take: Estradiol above about 200 pg/mL turns feedback positive, and the LH surge that follows triggers ovulation, about 14 days before menses.

hints.quote: As the follicle's developing, inhibin levels go up. And inhibin, remember, is going to preferentially inhibit FSH. So that's why we don't call it an LH-FSH surge, we call it an LH surge.
hints.take: FSH does rise at midcycle, a smaller peak than LH's (as in Dr. Herr's L14 graph), because inhibin from the follicle holds it back at the anterior pituitary.

hints.quote: The reason the LH surge is so important is because these pre-ovulatory Graafian follicles have high expression of LH receptors.
hints.take: The surge acts on that follicle three ways: proteases such as collagenase weaken its wall, prostaglandins raise its blood flow, and oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) falls, so meiosis I resumes and is finished by ovulation.

hints.quote: So, progesterone's high, you see changes in body temperature, because progesterone stimulates elevated body temperature in the hypothalamus.
hints.take: A slight rise in body temperature is a luteal-phase feature, from progesterone acting on the hypothalamus.

hints.quote: Whole body actions of the steroid hormones, this is not test... I'm not gonna test you on this.
hints.take: Skip slide 33 (estrogen and progesterone on the skin, memory, mammary glands, GI motility, the brain and the heart). The menopause slide's symptoms right after it still count.

hints.quote: You see a kind of an increase, a real high spike in GnRH, LH, and FSH, because we're losing the brake, we're losing that negative feedback regulation.
hints.take: Menopause: the follicles are gone, so no estradiol (or inhibin) and no negative feedback; GnRH, LH and FSH all rise. Hot flashes have been linked to the GnRH peak, though he said the research is still going on.

hints.quote: So what you need to understand is that if we don't have those elements, if we don't have testosterone, we don't have DHT, and we don't have anti-Müllerian hormone. The default pathway is female reproductive development.
hints.take: No AMH: the Müllerian ducts form the fallopian tubes and uterus. No testosterone: the Wolffian ducts regress. No DHT: the external genitalia form as female.

hints.quote: Prolactin is a negative signal to GnRH.
hints.take: Primary amenorrhea is usually genetic (his example: Turner syndrome, an X partly or completely lost, malformed ovaries). Secondary amenorrhea: menopause, pregnancy, lactation and hyperprolactinemia (a pituitary tumor), the last two because prolactin turns GnRH down.

hints.quote: Exam 2's five Exam 1 questions will come from L2, L3, L6 and L10.
hints.take: From the class, 11/11: L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary, L3 Endocrinology of Growth, L6 Adrenal Gland and L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation. The Refresher's High Likelihood questions, its notes and cram sheet, Exam 1 High likelihood in the Question Bank and the mock's five are those four lectures now. The other Exam 1 lectures' questions came out of the hub.

dmpharm: Every drug that releases insulin (insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides) causes hypoglycemia and weight gain.
Metformin is first-line for type 2; it cuts hepatic gluconeogenesis and doesn't lower a normal glucose.
Metformin: GI upset (fades in 1 to 2 weeks), low B12, lactic acidosis; absolutely contraindicated below eGFR 30.
Weight problem: GLP-1 agonist first. Heart failure on a diuretic: SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin is approved for heart failure).
TZDs (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone): PPAR-gamma, a nuclear receptor; edema, weight gain, heart failure, macular edema; avoid in NYHA III and IV and ALT over 2.5 times normal.

Sulfonylureas close the beta cell K-ATP channel: depolarization, calcium in, insulin out; they need working beta cells, and low durability means the dose climbs after 1 to 2 years until they stop working.
Sulfonylurea warnings: G6PD deficiency, liver, kidney (mostly glyburide), disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
Meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide): peak and half-life about 1 hour, with meals; not after a sulfonylurea fails.
Rapid insulins (lispro, aspart, glulisine): onset 5 to 15 minutes, last about 4 hours; regular peaks about 3 hours, gone by 8; NPH onset 2 to 4 hours.
Basal: glargine (more than 24 hours, no peak), detemir; ultra-long degludec (more than 42 hours). Inhaled Afrezza: 1 to 2 minutes.
Regular and NPH are sold without a prescription. Insulin adverse effects: hypoglycemia, weight gain, transient worse retinopathy, lipoatrophy or lipohypertrophy.
GLP-1 agonists: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon, slower gastric emptying, weight loss; boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors.
GLP-1 agonists slow the absorption of oral contraceptives and antibiotics; oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) is the one tablet.
DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins): oral, daily, no hypoglycemia, weight neutral, modest; avoid in heart failure except sitagliptin; linagliptin needs no renal adjustment.
SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins): glucosuria; genital yeast infections, UTIs, polyuria, hypotension; boxed warning for amputation (canagliflozin, ertugliflozin).
Acarbose and miglitol: block brush-border alpha-glucosidase; flatulence, bloating, diarrhea; no hypoglycemia.
Pramlintide: synthetic amylin, SC before meals, type 1 or 2; hypoglycemia with insulin.
C-peptide is made 1:1 with your own insulin; absent C-peptide means no insulin of your own.
Diagnosis needs two: A1C 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 or more, 2-hour OGTT 200 or more, random above 200. Prediabetes: A1C 5.7 to 6.4, fasting 100 to 125.
Hypoglycemia in the chair: awake gets juice, regular soda or glucose tablets; unresponsive gets glucagon (injection or nasal).
path1: Opposite directions = primary: T4 high, TSH low (Graves); T4 low, TSH high (Hashimoto).
Same direction = secondary: both high (TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma); both low (failed pituitary, e.g. Sheehan).
Anterior pituitary = secretory epithelium; posterior = unmyelinated nerve fibers + pituicytes storing ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.
5 cell types, 7 hormones: corticotrophs (ACTH, MSH) and gonadotrophs (FSH, LH) make two each. TRH releases TSH and prolactin; dopamine stops prolactin; somatostatin stops GH.
Microadenoma under 10 mm; macroadenoma over 10 mm, with mass effect: big sella, nausea and vomiting, headache, bitemporal hemianopsia (crossing central fibers).
Prolactinoma: most common hyperfunctioning tumor; amenorrhea-galactorrhea; micro in premenopausal women.
Somatotroph: largest adenomas; gigantism (child) vs acromegaly (adult); glucose intolerance, osteoporosis, hypertension.
Corticotroph: ACTH, Cushing disease, micro. Gonadotroph: no syndrome, found by mass effect, 10-20% of macroadenomas.
Hypopituitarism needs about 75% loss. Sheehan = postpartum ischemic necrosis (can't breastfeed). Null cell adenoma. Empty sella (obese multiparous women).
Central DI: no ADH; polyuria, low urine specific gravity, high serum sodium. Nephrogenic: normal ADH, kidneys ignore it. Oxytocin: no syndrome.
SIADH: hyponatremia; most common cause is ectopic ADH from small cell lung carcinoma.
Thyroid starts at the back of the tongue: lingual thyroid, thyroglossal duct cyst, substernal gland. C cells make calcitonin.
Graves: most common endogenous hyperthyroidism; IgG STIMULATES the TSH receptor; diffuse hyperplasia, goiter, ophthalmopathy; women 5:1.
Hashimoto (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis): most common hypothyroidism in the US; as taught, antibodies BLOCK the TSH receptor; lymphocytes, larger nuclei, pinker cytoplasm.
Myxedema: weight gain, cold, sluggish, coarse face, ENLARGED TONGUE, puffy hands. Cretinism: child, short, slow development, big head, big tongue.
Follicular carcinoma: capsular or vascular invasion; RAS; blood to lung and bone; women ~50; widely invasive = 4+ vessels; hemithyroidectomy enough.
Papillary: 60-80%, under 40, radiation, BRAF, lymphatics, multifocal (total thyroidectomy), pale grooved nuclei, pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies in 50%, 10-year survival over 80%.
Medullary: C cells, RET, MEN 2A/2B; sporadic 80% (solitary, 45) vs familial (35, bilateral, C-cell hyperplasia); amyloid; calcitonin, chromogranin, CEA.
Anaplastic: 10%, age 60-80, endemic goiter areas, rapidly fatal neck mass, undifferentiated; urgent molecular testing (BRAF target).
path2: PTH takes back calcium and dumps phosphate (and makes 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D); aldosterone takes back sodium and dumps potassium.
Active PTH (intact, N-terminal) lasts minutes, liver and kidney; inactive C-terminal lasts hours, glomerular filtration.
Parathyroids sit BEHIND the thyroid. Chief cells clear to bluish, oxyphils pink. Percent cells is about 100 minus age (70 percent fat at 70).
Primary hyperparathyroidism: calcium high, PTH high, phosphate low. Most are asymptomatic now. Stones, bones and groans.
Adenoma 80 to 90 percent (solitary, lower gland, women 3 to 1, 0.3 to 1.0 g); hyperplasia 10 to 15 percent (all four, 1 to 3 g); carcinoma very rare (calcium over 13, invasive, necrosis).
Labs can't separate adenoma from hyperplasia: count the enlarged glands.
One gland: remove it, biopsy a normal one. Several: remove three and a half.
Sestamibi: everything lit at 15 minutes, only the bad gland at 2 hours. Intraoperative PTH: drop of more than 50 percent in 15 to 20 minutes = success.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism: chronic low calcium; renal failure most common; all glands hyperplastic; milder; fix the cause.
Hypoparathyroidism: calcium low, phosphate high, PTH low. Thyroidectomy, DiGeorge, autoimmune. Chvostek (tap cheek) and Trousseau (cuff on arm). Dental root hypoplasia.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism: PTH HIGH, calcium low, phosphate high; end-organ resistance; short stature, short metacarpals. Rule out renal failure, malabsorption, vitamin D deficiency.
Cortex from the outside in: glomerulosa (salt, aldosterone), fasciculata (sugar, cortisol), reticularis (sex, androgens). Medulla: catecholamines.
Cushing: cortisol and ACTH both high = pituitary or ectopic (lung) ACTH; cortisol high, ACTH low = adrenal tumor.
Conn (primary): aldosterone high, renin LOW. Secondary (CHF, renal artery stenosis): aldosterone high, renin HIGH.

CAH: autosomal recessive, cortisol-synthesis enzyme. 21-hydroxylase: androgen excess, a third waste sodium. 17-hydroxylase: androgen deficiency, sodium retention, hypertension. Treat all with glucocorticoids.
Addison: everything low but ACTH; sodium low, potassium high, glucose low, hypotension, hyperpigmentation. Autoimmune 60 to 70 percent.
Cortical adenoma: mostly nonsecreting, functional ones mostly aldosterone. Carcinoma: large, 50 percent functional; most virilizing adrenal tumors.
Pheochromocytoma: chromaffin cells, catecholamines, attacks of sweating, palpitations, hypertension. Rule of 10s. Zellballen.
Neuroblastoma: very aggressive, 80 percent under 5, sympathetic chain, abdomen most often, spreads to bone, liver, lung, nodes. Adults: olfactory neuroblastoma in the roof of the nose.
mhisto: On the exam (he said so): his labeled Sertoli cell drawing. Basal lamina → type A, type B spermatogonia (basal) → junctional complex → primary spermatocyte → early → late spermatid at the lumen (adluminal).
Testis: thick tunica albuginea, septa → about 250 lobules, each with several blind-ended, coiled seminiferous tubules; Leydig cells sit in the connective tissue between tubules.
Tubule wall: connective tissue + peritubular myoid cells. Epithelium: only Sertoli cells + spermatogenic cells.
Spermatogenesis needs a lower temperature (scrotum): about 35°C on his slide, not 37°C; about 200 million sperm a day; about 74 days per round. (Dr. Madison's L15: about 34°C and about two months.)
LH → Leydig → testosterone. FSH → Sertoli → androgen-binding protein. Testosterone lowers LH; inhibin blocks FSH.
Sertoli: tall columnar, basement membrane to lumen, ovoid nucleus; tight junctions = blood-testis barrier (basal vs adluminal).
Sertoli makes ABP, inhibin, anti-Müllerian hormone; phagocytoses shed cytoplasm; no division in the adult; resists heat, radiation, toxins.
Leydig: outside the tubules; testosterone in the embryo, at maturity and to maintain spermatogenesis.
Dark A = reserve stem cell (vacuole, peripheral nucleolus). Pale A = progenitor (no vacuole, central nucleolus). Type B → primary spermatocyte → adluminal.
Meiosis: diploid primary spermatocyte → haploid spermatids. Spermiogenesis: spermatid → spermatozoon. Spermiation: release from the Sertoli cell.
Spermiogenesis: nucleus → head; Golgi → acrosome; mitochondria → middle piece; flagellum forms; phases: Golgi, cap/acrosomal, maturation.
Path: seminiferous tubule → tubuli recti → rete testis (cuboidal, mediastinum) → 10 to 12 efferent ductules → epididymis → vas → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
Efferent ductules: non-ciliated cuboidal (absorb fluid) alternating with ciliated columnar (sweep sperm). Real cilia.
Epididymis: coiled 4 to 6 m, pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia + basal cells (precursors of the columnar cells); matures (2 to 12 days), stores, moves by peristalsis.
Epididymal maturation: chromatin stabilized, membrane charge changed, new surface proteins, forward motility. Glycerophosphocholine inhibits capacitation.

Vas deferens: straight, thick muscular wall, stereocilia; in the spermatic cord with the testicular artery and pampiniform plexus (the only two cord parts he said to know). Vas + seminal vesicle duct → ejaculatory duct, through the prostate.
Seminal vesicles: about 70% of semen (L15: 50 to 80%), fructose (energy), prostaglandins; yellow lipochrome fluoresces in UV light (forensics).

Prostate: wraps the urethra (enlarged → trouble urinating); 30 to 50 glands (mucosal, submucosal, main), fibromuscular stroma; citric acid, acid phosphatase, fibrinolysin, PSA; alkaline first portion; corpora amylacea increase with age.
Bulbourethral (Cowper's): galactose + sialic acid mucus into the penile urethra, before emission; skeletal muscle between units = somatic (voluntary) control.

Erection = smooth muscle RELAXES → the two corpora cavernosa fill → veins compressed against the tunica albuginea. Urethra in the corpus spongiosum, which fills little and stays open. Point (parasympathetic) and shoot (sympathetic).
fhisto: Every follicle holds a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I; the LH surge finishes meiosis I just before ovulation.
The ovulated cell is a secondary oocyte arrested at metaphase II; only fertilization finishes meiosis II (ovum plus second polar body).
Unequal cytokinesis: one big oocyte, one tiny polar body.
Oocytes: 5 to 7 million by the 5th fetal month, 1 to 2 million at birth, about 400,000 at menarche, about 450 ovulated.
About 12 follicles start each month; one dominant follicle ovulates; the rest are atretic (apoptosis).
Primordial: one layer of squamous cells, desmosomes, oocyte about 25 micrometers.
Early primary: one layer of cuboidal granulosa cells, zona starting. Late primary: several layers, theca forming.
Secondary follicle = liquor folliculi (made under FSH) and an antrum; cumulus oophorus and corona radiata.
Graafian follicle: about 20 mm, bulges on the ovary; primordial to Graafian takes many months (he stressed it). Wall from the antrum out: granulosa, basement membrane, theca interna, theca externa.
Granulosa cells: gap junctions, no tight junctions, so no blood-follicle barrier (the testis has one).
Theca interna: vascular, LH receptors, androgens (estrogen precursors). Theca externa: fibrous tissue and smooth muscle.
FSH surge grows 10 to 12 antral follicles; LH (the FSH plus LH surge) matures and ovulates the dominant one.
Estrogen from the Graafian follicle triggers the LH surge: theca interna edema, meiosis-inducing factor, rupture through the tunica albuginea.
Granulosa-lutein cells make progesterone and estrogen; theca-lutein cells (from theca interna) make progesterone.
No pregnancy: corpus luteum becomes a corpus albicans (fibroblasts, collagen). Pregnancy: a placental hormone maintains it.
Cycle: menstrual 1-5, proliferative (follicular) 5-14, secretory (luteal) 15-28.
His graph: ovulation days 13-15; estrogen peaks day 12-13; FSH and LH peak together just before ovulation; progesterone peaks about day 22.
Progesterone drop, spiral arteries constrict, functionalis hypoxic and shed; the basalis has its own straight arteries, stays and regrows it.
Tube: ampulla = fertilization; ciliated cells beat toward the uterus; peg cells feed the ovum; mucosa promotes capacitation; oocyte lives about 24 h.
Cervix: mucous columnar crypts; watery at ovulation, viscous plug in pregnancy; transformation zone to stratified squamous.
Vagina: stratified squamous, no glands; glycogen to lactic acid by Lactobacillus keeps pathogens down.
Milk: prolactin makes it, oxytocin ejects it; colostrum (3 to 4 days) has more protein and IgA.
mphys: 4 G's: genetic (XY/XX), gonadal (testes/ovaries), phenotypic or genital (penis/vagina), gender (identity).

Sertoli AMH removes the Müllerian ducts; Leydig testosterone (hCG, LH) builds the Wolffian structures (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles); DHT (5-alpha-reductase) builds penis, scrotum, prostate.

Androgen insensitivity: androgen receptor mutated or absent (often X-linked); XY, testes stay internal, no uterus or ovaries, no Wolffian ducts, blind-ended vagina, female puberty (breasts, little body hair).
5-alpha-reductase deficiency: XY, testes, Wolffian ducts present, no Müllerian ducts, female genitalia; raised as girls, virilize at puberty (often how it's found).

Sertoli (FSH, tubule wall): nourish, blood-testis barrier (tight junctions; immune privilege), fluid, ABP, spermiation, inhibin, aromatase, phagocytose bad sperm; AMH in the fetus. He said Sertoli vs Leydig is where he would study.
Leydig (LH, interstitium): testosterone from cholesterol; LH turns up cholesterol desmolase, as ACTH does in the adrenal.
ABP keeps testosterone in the testis higher than in the blood.
Spermatogenesis is optimal at 34 degrees Celsius (said in class; L13 histology: about 35); warm, testes drop; cold, dartos tightens the scrotum; heat passes artery to vein.
One spermatocyte, two meiotic divisions, four spermatids with 23 unpaired chromosomes; spermatids mature about two months (L13 histology: about 74 days for the whole process).
Epididymis: sperm arrive non-motile; capable after 18 to 24 hours; gain motility, forward motility proteins, acrosomal stabilizing factors; stored for months.
Acrosome: from the Golgi; hyaluronidase and proteolytic enzymes.
Rate-limiting step for testosterone: P450 side-chain cleavage (desmolase).
Aromatase: testosterone to estradiol, androstenedione to estrone; mostly Sertoli cells (FSH) from fetal life on, some Leydig (he crossed out the slide's "Leydig in adults").
Testosterone inhibits GnRH (hypothalamus) and LH (pituitary); inhibin (Sertoli) inhibits FSH, at the pituitary only.
Testosterone across life: high in the fetus, a peak after birth, quiet in childhood, surge at puberty, steady (not cyclic) in adults, decline in old age.
GnRH must pulse: continuous GnRH lowers LH and testosterone.
Labs: failing testes = low T, high LH and FSH; failing pituitary = all low; injected T = high T, low LH and FSH, low sperm count.

Seminal vesicles: 60 to 70 percent of the fluid (slide 50 to 80), fructose, prostaglandins (female tract contractions), fibrinogen (the clot). Prostate: 20 to 30 percent, thin milky fluid, citrate, calcium, PSA breaks the clot. Cowper's: lubricating mucus first.
Point (erection, lubrication) = parasympathetic; shoot (emission, ejaculation) = sympathetic.
Erection: ACh and NO dilate the cavernosal arteries; guanylate cyclase, cGMP, smooth muscle relaxes, veins compressed.
Sildenafil blocks PDE5 (cGMP breakdown); no direct effect, needs sexual stimulation.
fphys: Female tract = default pathway: no Y, no testes, no AMH (Müllerian ducts form the tubes and uterus), no testosterone (Wolffian ducts regress), no DHT (female external genitalia).
GnRH → portal system → anterior pituitary → FSH and LH → ovary makes estrogen and inhibin.

KNDy (kisspeptin) neurons relay stress, nutrition, metabolism (leptin) and inflammation to GnRH neurons; GnRH neurons don't sense them directly. Leptin turns GnRH up; stress, inflammation, hypoglycemia and prolactin turn it down.
Progesterone: negative feedback only. Estrogen: negative, or positive above about 200 pg/mL. Inhibin: suppresses FSH.
Positive feedback makes the female cyclical; the male has none and is acyclical.

Two cells, two gonadotropins ("very important slide"): LH → theca → cholesterol desmolase (P450scc, rate-limiting, cholesterol → pregnenolone) → testosterone; FSH → granulosa → aromatase → 17β-estradiol. The only two enzymes he said to know.

Theca ≈ Leydig (no aromatase; testosterone moves to the granulosa); granulosa ≈ Sertoli. Granulosa cells add LH receptors at midcycle. FSH rises a little with the LH surge; inhibin keeps its peak small (Dr. Madison and Dr. Herr agree).
17β-estradiol = main ovarian estrogen; estrone = menopause (adrenal DHEA, zona reticularis); estriol = pregnancy (fetal 16-OH-DHEA-S, placenta).
Follicles are in the cortex; vessels in the medulla and hilum.

Primary follicle: single cuboidal granulosa layer, FSH receptors. Secondary: multiple layers + theca, theca interna LH receptors. Graafian: antrum. (L14 names: late primary, then secondary for the antral follicle.)
No follicle moves past stage 1 before puberty: up to 13-50 years of waiting. A few start each cycle; one becomes dominant.
Meiosis I is finished by ovulation (the LH surge lowers oocyte maturation inhibitor, OMI); meiosis II is finished in the fallopian tube, only if fertilized (L14).
Follicular (proliferative) days 0-14, estrogen. Luteal (secretory) days 14-28, progesterone, corpus luteum. (L14 counts menstrual 1-5, proliferative 5-14, secretory 15-28.)

High yield: follicular works toward fertilization (lining grows, watery, stretchy mucus helps sperm); luteal toward implantation (proliferation slows, vessels and glycogen up, thick mucus, body temperature slightly up).
Ovulation = 14 days before menses; egg out 24-36 h after the LH surge; collagenases weaken the wall, prostaglandins raise blood flow.
Corpus luteum: mostly granulosa cells; placenta takes over if fertilized; otherwise regresses over 14 days into the corpus albicans.
Menses: corpus luteum regression → abrupt loss of estrogen and progesterone.
Estrogen: endometrial growth, arteries lengthen, watery mucus, myometrium contracts. Progesterone: secretions and vessels up, thick mucus, myometrium relaxes.

Menopause: complete atresia, no estradiol or inhibin → GnRH, LH, FSH up; the GnRH peak is linked to hot flashes; estrone dominant (adrenal DHEA, much weaker); bone loss, thin vaginal epithelium, less breast mass.

Secondary amenorrhea: pregnancy, lactation, menopause, hyperprolactinemia (prolactin turns GnRH down). Primary: usually genetic; Turner syndrome (an X lost, malformed ovaries), which the slide files as a disorder of sexual differentiation.
Skip (he said): the steroid pathway's other enzymes, the in-between follicle names, the whole-body actions slide.
refresh: Five of the fifty questions are on Exam 1 material: L2, L3, L6 and L10 only
L2: three hormone types: peptides (stored, surface receptors), amines, steroids (made on demand, cholesterol from LDL, intracellular receptors)
L2: know Gs, Gi, Gq plus the insulin (RTK) and GH (JAK2) receptors
L2: primary: target hormone and pituitary hormone move opposite; secondary: same direction
L2: the posterior pituitary makes no hormones; dopamine holds prolactin down
L3: GHRH (Gs) raises GH; somatostatin (Gi, hyperpolarizes) lowers it: yin-yang
L3: main feedback: GH and IGF-1 raise hypothalamic somatostatin
L3: GH is diabetogenic and lipolytic; builds muscle protein
L3: gigantism before plate closure; acromegaly after (jaw, brow, hands)
L3: somatopause: from the 30s, smaller and shorter pulses; the weak link is GHRH, not the somatotrophs
L6: glomerulosa: aldosterone (only zone with aldosterone synthase)
L6: aldosterone: ENaC + Na/K pump: keep Na, lose K
L6: Addison's: high ACTH + MSH → pigmented gums
L10: CaSR is Gq; rising intracellular Ca INHIBITS PTH (the paradox)
L10: PTH: keep Ca, dump phosphate; bone via osteoblasts; net Ca up, P down
L10: PTH receptor on osteoblasts, NOT osteoclasts; calcitonin acts on osteoclasts
L10: primary hyperparathyroidism: high PTH and Ca, low P, kidney stones
